lines.text: Systems of linear equations! Every SAT has them, and most students waste two minutes doing algebra they don't even need.
Graph two lines. Different slopes? They cross once. Here, x plus y equals eight and two x minus y equals four collide right at four, four. One solution.
Now lock them to the exact same slope, with different intercepts. Parallel tracks! They never touch. Zero solutions.
What if the second equation is just the first one times two? Same slope, same intercept. One line disguised as two: infinitely many solutions.
When you do need the point, stack them and add! Plus y and minus y vaporize on contact.
Three x equals twelve, so x is four. Plug it back in: y is four. Ten seconds flat.
Now watch this classic SAT trap: twelve x minus a y equals ten, and four x minus three y equals negative five. What value of a gives no solution?
No solution means parallel, so the x and y coefficients must scale together! Multiply the bottom row by three to match twelve x.
Four times three is twelve, so three times three gives a equals nine! Boom, parallel lines, zero solutions.
Test yourself on the practice problems right after this in SAT Math Learner.
